query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a slight Al doping into FeNiCrCoCu promotes stable protective oxide film formation under high-temperature sliding, reducing friction and local plastic deformation by preventing severe oxidative and adhesive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline thin coating of FeNiCrCoCu on a steel substrate with no Al addition.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small Al addition (e.g., ~2 at.%) into the FeNiCrCoCu thin coating.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (600–800 °C) pin-on-disk wear tests under identical load and sliding speed for both the baseline and Al-doped coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable Al-rich oxide tribofilm and refined near-surface microstructure during elevated-temperature sliding.
generation.mechanism: Al doping enhances the nucleation of protective oxide layers at high temperatures, thereby reducing oxide breakage and mitigating substrate material removal and sub-surface distortion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped coating, the Al-doped FeNiCrCoCu exhibits lower wear rates and reduced depth of plastic deformation in the high-temperature sliding regime.
generation.baseline: Undoped FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on steel, tested at 600–800 °C under identical wear conditions.
generation.boundary: This benefit is expected primarily in oxidation-dominated regimes above ~600 °C; excessive Al (>5–10 at.%) may worsen ductility and reduce tribological gains.
generation.uncertainty: Exact dopant levels, secondary phase formation, and long-term durability under cyclic temperature and load are not yet clearly established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare baseline FeNiCrCoCu and Al-doped (e.g., ~2 at.%) coatings by the same deposition method on identical steel substrates. Perform sliding wear tests at 600–800 °C, measuring friction, mass loss, and wear track profiles. Characterize oxide films with SEM/EDS.
measurements: Wear rate, friction coefficient, and mass loss under repeated loading cycles
Near-surface microhardness for each coating system
Microstructural and chemical analysis of the worn surfaces for oxide film presence and thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no appreciable Al-enriched oxide forms, or if measured wear rate and plastic deformation do not decrease for the Al-doped coating relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

AbstractTo enhance the friction and wear properties of 40Cr steel’s surface, CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings with various Ti contents were prepared using laser cladding. X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) were used to characterize the phase composition, microstructure, and chemical composition of the samples. The findings demonstrated that the CoCrFeMnNiTix HEA coatings formed a single FCC phase. Fe2Ti, Ni3Ti, and Co2Ti intermetallic compounds were discovered in the coatings when the molar ratio of Ti content was greater than 0.5. The EDS findings indicated that Cr and Co/Ni/Ti were primarily enriched in the dendrite and interdendrite, respectively. Ti addition can effectively enhance the coating’s mechanical properties. The hardness test findings showed that when the molar ratio of Ti was 0.75, the coating’s microhardness was 511 HV0.5, which was 1.9 times the hardness of the 40Cr (256 HV0.5) substrate and 1.46 times the hardness of the CrCrFeMnNi HEA coating (348 HV0.5). The friction and wear findings demonstrated that the addition of Ti can substantially reduce the coating’s friction coefficient and

SEM and 3D morphology test results demonstrated that the coating’s wear mechanism changed from adhesive wear and abrasive wear to fatigue wear and abrasive wear with the increase in Ti content.Keywords: laser cladding, high-entropy alloy, CoCrFeMnNiTi, microstructure, friction and wear

occupying_moves.lever: Slight Al doping of the baseline FeNiCrCoCu composition
occupying_moves.technique: High-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., pin-on-disk) coupled with cross-sectional electron microscopy and compositional analysis
occupying_moves.conditions: Thin coatings on steel substrates; baseline vs. Al-doped FeNiCrCoCu coatings tested at 600–800 °C under identical load and sliding speed

chosen.lever: Slight Al doping of FeNiCrCoCu coating
chosen.technique: High-temperature tribological testing plus microstructural/chemical characterization (SEM, EDS, TEM)
chosen.conditions: FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings with or without Al doping on steel, tested at 600–800 °C under equivalent loads and sliding conditions
chosen.why: Introducing a small amount of Al is a direct and standard composition adjustment that can promote stable oxide formation at high temperature. Comparing wear rates, friction, and microstructural evolution of Al-doped vs. baseline coatings will most directly test whether the hypothesized role of high-temperature oxide film formation governs wear resistance and microscopic deformation. Demonstrating no reduction in wear or no improvement in deformation resistance upon Al doping would falsify this mechanism.
